title: Mortgage refinancing game has changed
full_text:
With mortgage rates hitting their highest level in 18 years, refinancing is expected to surge as stretched households seek out ways to relieve mounting cost pressures.
But the game has changed somewhat since the last bout of refinancing gripped the market, when interest rates bounced higher from the near zero levels reached during the Covid pandemic.
Back in 2023, amid a reviving property market, many bank customers found they did not need to switch banks to get a better deal on their home loan. All they had to do was utter three magic words: mortgage discharge authority.
That simple term had bank retention staff instantly promising better terms to hold onto customers. But the banks are getting sharper in their approach, according to Loan Market head of content Shay Waraker.
“What we are hearing from our brokers is that the big banks are now waiting to see if a customer is serious about quitting their loan,” Waraker says.
“They will wait until their clients have actually completed a mortgage discharge and only then make efforts to reclaim them for the bank with a better deal.” Loan Market is a major player in the mortgage market, with about 700 mortgage brokers.
Waraker says there was a 7 per cent increase month-on-month to the end of October in customers refinancing mortgages. She says the figure would move higher. “I think we are going to see more people trying to free up cash to avoid making drastic decisions,” she says.
Competition in the mortgage market is heating up as banks compete for fewer loans, with the property downturn continuing to spook buyers from transacting, while higher interest rates are making it difficult for other buyers to gain a loan altogether.
The looming upswing in refinancing is already clear from the lending volumes at the banks where the majority – 57 per cent of new lending – is refinancing.
New rates reality For anyone testing the waters on a new deal, comparison website Canstar says that, after this week’s RBA rate rise, borrowers can forget about rates below 6 per cent, with the average for owner-occupiers at 6.74 per cent and for investors at 6.97 per cent.
A Canstar survey showed one in 10 borrowers would be unable to meet higher repayments, while a further 28 per cent said they would struggle.
Canstar data insights director Sally Tindall says there is a growing divide between borrowers who could absorb another rate rise and those who could not stretch their budgets any further.
“For someone with a $600,000 mortgage, repayments are now set to be around $456 a month higher than they were at the start of the year,” Tindall says.
Rates are changing constantly, and the lowest rates invariably have set conditions. Among the best this week are products from Virgin Money, Unloan, BCU Bank and Transport Mutual, with rates still about 6.1 per cent.
Refinancing strategies If you do want to refinance, what are the key factors in making that decision? It’s best to see if your bank will improve your existing loan, but if they can’t or it still remains uncompetitive, refinancing with a new bank should be considered.
However, refinancing can involve more than just seeking a lower headline interest rate in order to reduce repayments.
Rasti Vaibhav, the CEO of the Get Rare buyer’s agency, started his career as an analyst for Westpac, and says there are three key ways to refinance your mortgage: ● Moving to a new deal with a distinctly lower rate; ● Lengthening the time frame of a mortgage (and paying less in mortgage costs per month), and; ● Optimising mortgage offset accounts by restructuring existing loans to free up cashflow that will cushion you from a future cost squeeze.
Vaibhav says refinancing needs to be carried out with the big picture in mind: “It’s important to know the different ways you can refinance; it’s also important not to place too much emphasis on the headline rates.
“There are other factors, and you need to do your numbers to make sure it works for you.” He says if people are refinancing with their own bank, there are new charges they will face with any new loan arrangement – and those new costs must be built into the estimated outcome.
Vaibhav says the other less well-known refinancing strategies could better reward borrowers. For example, more banks are willing to let mortgages run out to 35-40 years. This means a borrower could stay with their bank but restructure their loan arrangement so that their mortgage costs less per fortnight.
“In taking this option, you must understand in the fullness of time that if you were to repay this loan through the period you would hand more money over to the bank, but it can be very useful in the medium term,” he says.
He also says some mortgage holders could consider a strategy involving a mortgage offset. It is used by property owners who have found it difficult to make mortgage repayments but they have built up substantial equity in a property.
Vaibhav says those borrowers may have a loan-to-value ratio considerably lower than what the bank requires. To ease their mortgage stress, they could make the unlikely move of borrowing more against the property and placing the funds in a mortgage offset. The move to bolster the offset account funds creates a cash buffer so that, whatever else occurs, the borrower can keep meeting the requirements to hold onto the property. “The caveat here is that you must not use that money for anything else; this is optimising your equity in the home by creating a buffer for a period when rates are higher than you ever expected,” Vaibhav says.
